name: Zero-Sum Bias
description: People can intuitively read a situation as win-lose even when the resource is not actually fixed. One person's gain feels like it must come out of someone else's share, even in genuinely non-zero-sum systems.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to marketplaces, creator ecosystems, grading/ranking UI, workplace tooling, and fairness debates: teams or users may assume another person's gain necessarily harms them, which distorts policy, prioritization, and communication choices.
prevalence_note: Explicitly named in social-psychology and fairness/redistribution discussions, and relevant to some marketplace or workplace-design debates, but not a mainstream everyday UX law.

findings.description: A 12-study program (4 main experiments, 8 supplementary) found that people pervasively deny the mutually beneficial nature of voluntary economic exchanges, judging buyers as less likely to benefit than sellers even in simple, symmetric goods/services transactions -- a form of zero-sum misperception ('win-win denial') distinct from and independent of Meegan's (2010) academic-grading paradigm. Traced to mercantilist theories of value (confusing wealth for money) and theory-of-mind limits, rather than to the intra-group-competition heuristic Meegan's grading study invoked -- an independent demonstration of zero-sum thinking through a different mechanism and paradigm (economic exchange judgment), closing this topic's single-study-risk gap and adding direct relevance to marketplace and creator-ecosystem design, where buyer/seller or creator/platform gains are often misjudged as mutually exclusive.
findings.source_title: Win–win denial: The psychological underpinnings of zero-sum thinking

findings.description: Across three experiments in an objectively non-zero-sum grading environment, participants predicted poorer outcomes for later students after seeing many earlier high grades, indicating that they intuitively perceived competition for limited desirable resources even when no such limit existed.
findings.source_title: Zero-Sum Bias: Perceived Competition Despite Unlimited Resources
